feature.description:
The iptables mode of kube-proxy now tracks accepted packets that are destined for node-ports on localhost by introducing `kubeproxy_iptables_localhost_nodeports_accepted_packets_total` metric.
This will help users to identify if they rely on iptables.localhostNodePorts feature and ulitmately help them to migrate from iptables to nftables.
feature.author: aroradaman
feature.userFacingChange:
The iptables mode of kube-proxy now tracks accepted packets that are destined for node-ports on localhost by introducing `kubeproxy_iptables_localhost_nodeports_accepted_packets_total` metric.
This will help users to identify if they rely on iptables.localhostNodePorts feature and ulitmately help them to migrate from iptables to nftables.

enrichment.problem: Users had no visibility into whether packets destined for node‑ports on localhost were being accepted when kube-proxy ran in iptables mode with the iptables.localhostNodePorts feature enabled. This made it difficult to know if the feature was in use and to safely migrate to nftables.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using kube-proxy in iptables mode with the iptables.localhostNodePorts feature enabled, especially those intending to switch to nftables.
enrichment.fix: A new Prometheus metric `kubeproxy_iptables_localhost_nodeports_accepted_packets_total` is added. In iptables mode, kube-proxy now increments this counter for each packet accepted for a localhost node‑port, exposing the usage of the localhostNodePorts feature.
enrichment.impact: Operators can now monitor the metric to detect reliance on iptables.localhostNodePorts, allowing them to verify usage and plan or validate migration to nftables without unexpected traffic loss.

feature.description: The feature-gate CSIMigrationPortworx was promoted to beta in Kubernetes 1.25, but turned off by default. In 1.31, it was turned on by default. Before upgrading to 1.31, please make sure that the corresponding portworx csi driver is installed if you are using Portworx.
feature.author: carlory
feature.userFacingChange: The feature-gate CSIMigrationPortworx was promoted to beta in Kubernetes 1.25, but turn it off by default. In 1.31, it was turned on by default. Before upgrading to 1.31, please make sure that the corresponding portworx csi driver is installed if you are using Portworx.

enrichment.problem: In Kubernetes 1.31 the CSIMigrationPortworx feature gate is enabled by default. Clusters that rely on the legacy in-tree Portworx volume plugin but have not installed the external Portworx CSI driver will experience volume provisioning failures after upgrade.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using Portworx storage without the Portworx CSI driver installed (i.e., those still using the in-tree volume plugin) are affected.
enrichment.fix: The default is changed to enable CSIMigrationPortworx. Users are advised to install the Portworx CSI driver before upgrading so that the migration from the in-tree plugin to the CSI driver occurs seamlessly.
enrichment.impact: Simplifies the migration to CSI for Portworx users by making it the default behavior, but requires pre‑upgrade installation of the CSI driver to avoid service disruption.

feature.description:
kubeadm: enabled the v1beta4 API. For a complete changelog since v1beta3 please see https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/kubeadm-config.v1beta4/. 

The API does include a few breaking changes:
- The "extraArgs" component construct is now a list of "name"/"value" pairs instead of a string/string map. This has been done to support duplicate args where needed.
- The "JoinConfiguration.discovery.timeout" field has been replaced by "JoinConfiguration.timeouts.discovery".
- The "ClusterConfiguration.timeoutForControlPlane" field has been replaced by "{Init|Join}Configuration.timeouts.controlPlaneComponentHealthCheck".
Please use the command "kubeadm config migrate" to migrate your existing v1beta3 configuration to v1beta4.

v1beta3 is now marked as deprecated but will continue to be supported until version 1.34 or later.
The storage configuration in the kube-system/kubeadm-config ConfigMap is now a v1beta4 ClusterConfiguration.
feature.author: neolit123
feature.userFacingChange:
kubeadm: enabled the v1beta4 API. For a complete changelog since v1beta3 please see https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/kubeadm-config.v1beta4/. 

The API does include a few breaking changes:
- The "extraArgs" component construct is now a list of "name"/"value" pairs instead of a string/string map. This has been done to support duplicate args where needed.
- The "JoinConfiguration.discovery.timeout" field has been replaced by "JoinConfiguration.timeouts.discovery".
- The "ClusterConfiguration.timeoutForControlPlane" field has been replaced by "{Init|Join}Configuration.timeouts.controlPlaneComponentHealthCheck".
Please use the command "kubeadm config migrate" to migrate your existing v1beta3 configuration to v1beta4.

v1beta3 is now marked as deprecated but will continue to be supported until version 1.34 or later.
The storage configuration in the kube-system/kubeadm-config ConfigMap is now a v1beta4 ClusterConfiguration.

enrichment.problem: The kubeadm configuration API v1beta4 introduces breaking changes: the extraArgs field is now a list of name/value pairs, and several timeout fields have been renamed (JoinConfiguration.discovery.timeout → JoinConfiguration.timeouts.discovery, ClusterConfiguration.timeoutForControlPlane → {Init|Join}Configuration.timeouts.controlPlaneComponentHealthCheck). Existing v1beta3 configs are incompatible.
enrichment.affected: Clusters initialized or joined with kubeadm using v1beta3 configuration files or the kube-system/kubeadm-config ConfigMap. Any automation/scripts that rely on the old extraArgs map or timeout fields are impacted.
enrichment.fix: kubeadm now enables the v1beta4 API and provides the "kubeadm config migrate" command to automatically convert v1beta3 configuration files and the kube-system/kubeadm-config ConfigMap to the new v1beta4 schema.
enrichment.impact: Users with existing kubeadm configuration files or ConfigMaps must run the migration tool to avoid errors during cluster init/join. The new list format for extraArgs allows duplicate arguments, improving flexibility.

feature.description:
`pause`: Added a `-v` flag to the Windows variant of the pause binary, which
prints the version of pause and exits. The Linux pause binary already has this flag.
feature.author: neolit123
feature.userFacingChange: pause: add a -v flag to the Windows variant of the pause binary, which prints the version of pause and exits. The Linux pause already has the flag.

enrichment.problem: The Windows variant of the pause binary lacked a -v flag, so users could not easily query its version, unlike the Linux variant which already supported this flag.
enrichment.affected: Windows nodes that run the pause container; operators who need to verify the pause binary version on Windows.
enrichment.fix: A -v flag was added to the Windows pause binary. When invoked, it prints the pause binary's version and exits.
enrichment.impact: Provides consistent behavior across Linux and Windows nodes, simplifying debugging and version verification for Windows workloads that rely on the pause container.

feature.description: Promoted the feature gate `KubeProxyDrainingTerminatingNodes` to stable
feature.author: alexanderConstantinescu

enrichment.problem: Kube-proxy handling of services on nodes that are terminating was only available behind the KubeProxyDrainingTerminatingNodes feature gate in beta, requiring manual enablement and lacking guaranteed stability.
enrichment.affected: Any cluster that runs kube-proxy and performs node termination or draining, especially workloads relying on continuous service traffic during node shutdown.
enrichment.fix: The KubeProxyDrainingTerminatingNodes feature gate is promoted to stable, making the draining behavior the default and guaranteeing stable semantics for terminating nodes.
enrichment.impact: Clusters no longer need to enable an alpha/beta gate to get reliable service traffic draining when nodes terminate, reducing potential service disruption during node shutdowns and simplifying cluster upgrades.

feature.description: The scheduler implements QueueingHint in VolumeBinding plugin's CSINode event, which enhances the throughput of scheduling.
feature.author: YamasouA

enrichment.problem: Scheduling throughput was limited because the VolumeBinding plugin did not efficiently handle CSINode events, causing slower pod placement in clusters that use CSI volumes.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use CSI drivers and the VolumeBinding plugin for dynamic volume provisioning experienced slower scheduling; the change benefits those workloads by speeding up pod placement.
enrichment.fix: Implemented the QueueingHint mechanism in the VolumeBinding plugin's CSINode event handling, allowing the scheduler to batch and prioritize these events, which increases scheduling throughput.
enrichment.impact: Improves the speed of pod scheduling, especially in environments with many CSI-backed volumes, reducing scheduling latency and increasing overall cluster efficiency.

feature.author: neolit123

a -v flag, to be on par with the Linux variant,

enrichment.problem: The Windows pause binary lacked the -v flag, so kubeadm could not perform the same simplified health check on Windows nodes as on Linux. The pause image used by clusters was still on an older version, causing inconsistency between Linux and Windows infrastructures.
enrichment.affected: Kubernetes clusters that run Windows nodes (especially those using kubeadm for cluster bootstrap and health checks).

feature.description:
Allowed creating ServiceAccount tokens bound to Node objects.
This allows users to bind a service account token's validity to a named Node object, similar to Pod bound tokens.
Use with `kubectl create token <serviceaccount-name> --bound-object-kind=Node --bound-object-node=<node-name>`.
feature.author: munnerz
feature.userFacingChange:
Allow creating ServiceAccount tokens bound to Node objects.
This allows users to bind a service account token's validity to a named Node object, similar to Pod bound tokens.
Use with `kubectl create token <serviceaccount-name> --bound-object-kind=Node --bound-object-node=<node-name>`.

enrichment.problem: ServiceAccount tokens could only be bound to Pods, preventing users from tying token validity to a specific Node for node‑scoped authentication scenarios.
enrichment.affected: Users who need node‑scoped ServiceAccount tokens, such as administrators configuring node‑level components or security policies.
enrichment.fix: Adds support for creating ServiceAccount tokens that are bound to a named Node object via the token request API and kubectl flag `--bound-object-kind=Node --bound-object-node=<node-name>`.
enrichment.impact: Enables node‑specific credential usage and tighter security controls, allowing workloads that run directly on a node (e.g., system components, node‑level agents) to use short‑lived, node‑bound ServiceAccount tokens.

feature.description: Graduated Kubernetes' support for AppArmor to GA. You now cannot disable the `AppArmor` feature gate.
feature.author: vinayakankugoyal
feature.userFacingChange: Graduate Kubernetes' support for AppArmor to GA.

enrichment.problem: AppArmor support was previously optional via a feature gate, allowing clusters to disable it. With the graduation to GA, the feature gate is now mandatory and cannot be turned off, which may break clusters that relied on disabling AppArmor or run on nodes without AppArmor support.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that previously disabled AppArmor via the feature gate, especially those running on Linux distributions without AppArmor support, will need to enable AppArmor on their nodes.
enrichment.fix: AppArmor support has been graduated to GA and the `AppArmor` feature gate is now always enabled. The code path that allowed disabling the gate has been removed.
enrichment.impact: Clusters must run on nodes with AppArmor enabled; otherwise pods may fail to start or run without security profiles. This provides consistent security enforcement across all clusters but requires users to ensure node compatibility.

feature.description: Promoted the `ProcMountType` feature gate to beta.
feature.author: sohankunkerkar
feature.userFacingChange: Promote ProcMountType feature to Beta

enrichment.problem: The procMount field, which controls how the /proc filesystem is mounted inside a container, was only available as an alpha feature behind a feature gate, preventing its use in production workloads.
enrichment.affected: Any pod that needs to control its /proc mount (e.g., security‑hardened workloads) and the node components that enforce the setting.
enrichment.fix: The ProcMountType feature gate has been promoted to beta, making the procMount field generally available and enabled by default in supported Kubernetes versions.
enrichment.impact: Clusters can now safely configure /proc mount behavior for pods, improving security isolation and allowing workloads that need specific /proc settings to run without custom feature‑gate handling.

feature.description:
Changed Linux swap handling to restrict access to swap for containers in high priority Pods.
New Pods that have a node- or cluster-critical priority are prohibited from accessing swap on Linux,
even if your cluster and node configuration could otherwise allow this.
feature.author: iholder101
feature.userFacingChange:
Changed Linux swap handling to restrict access to swap for containers in high priority Pods.
New Pods that have a node- or cluster-critical priority are prohibited from accessing swap on Linux,
even if your cluster and node configuration could otherwise allow this.

enrichment.problem: High‑priority Pods (node‑critical or cluster‑critical) could use swap on Linux when swap was enabled on the node, risking performance degradation or OOM for critical workloads.
enrichment.affected: Pods with node‑critical or cluster‑critical priority running on Linux nodes; any workloads that expected swap to be available to those Pods.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now blocks swap access for containers belonging to Pods with node‑critical or cluster‑critical priority on Linux, irrespective of the node or cluster swap configuration.
enrichment.impact: Critical workloads are protected from the latency and reliability issues caused by swap, making them more predictable. Users who relied on swap for high‑priority Pods must adjust their workloads or node configuration.

feature.description:
kube-scheduler implemented scheduling hints for the VolumeRestriction plugin.
Scheduling hints allow the scheduler to retry scheduling Pods that were previously rejected by the VolumeRestriction plugin if the Pod is deleted and the deleted Pod conflicts with the existing volumes of the current Pod.
feature.author: HirazawaUi
feature.userFacingChange:
kube-scheduler implements scheduling hints for the VolumeRestriction plugin.
Scheduling hints allow the scheduler to retry scheduling Pods that were previously rejected by the VolumeRestriction plugin if the Pod is deleted and the deleted Pod conflicts with the existing volumes of the current Pod.

enrichment.problem: Pods that were previously rejected by the VolumeRestriction plugin could not be rescheduled even after the conflicting pod was deleted, leading to unnecessary scheduling failures.
enrichment.affected: Pods that use volumes subject to the VolumeRestriction plugin, especially when a prior Pod using the same volume is deleted but its volume claim still caused a conflict.
enrichment.fix: kube-scheduler now supports scheduling hints for the VolumeRestriction plugin, allowing it to retry scheduling Pods that were rejected when a previously deleted Pod's volume conflict is resolved.
enrichment.impact: Reduces false‑negative scheduling rejections, improves pod startup reliability for workloads using volume restrictions, and decreases manual intervention needed to resolve scheduling deadlocks.

feature.description:
kube-scheduler implements scheduling hints for the VolumeRestriction plugin.
Scheduling hints allow the scheduler to retry scheduling Pods that were previously rejected by the VolumeRestriction plugin if a new pvc added, and the pvc belongs to pod.
feature.author: HirazawaUi
feature.userFacingChange:
kube-scheduler implements scheduling hints for the VolumeRestriction plugin.
Scheduling hints allow the scheduler to retry scheduling Pods that were previously rejected by the VolumeRestriction plugin if a new pvc added, and the pvc belongs to pod.

enrichment.problem: When a pod was rejected by the VolumeRestriction plugin because its required PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) did not exist yet, the scheduler would not attempt to schedule the pod again after the PVC was created, leaving the pod unscheduled.
enrichment.affected: Pods that are rejected by VolumeRestriction due to missing PVCs, particularly workloads that create PVCs after pod creation (e.g., multi‑step deployments).
enrichment.fix: kube-scheduler now implements scheduling hints for the VolumeRestriction plugin. The scheduler receives a hint when a new PVC belonging to a previously rejected pod appears and automatically retries scheduling that pod.
enrichment.impact: Pods that depend on PVCs created after the pod itself can now be scheduled automatically, eliminating the need for manual pod recreation and reducing deployment failures for workloads that create PVCs in separate steps.

feature.description:
Introduces new functionality to the dynamic client's `List` method, allowing users to enable API streaming. To activate this feature, users can set the `client-go.WatchListClient` feature gate.

It is important to note that the server must support streaming for this feature to function properly. If streaming is not supported by the server, the client will revert to using the normal `LIST` method to obtain data.
feature.author: p0lyn0mial
feature.userFacingChange:
Introduces new functionality to the dynamic client's `List` method, allowing users to enable API streaming. To activate this feature, users can set the `client-go.WatchListClient` feature gate.

It is important to note that the server must support streaming for this feature to function properly. If streaming is not supported by the server, the client will revert to using the normal `LIST` method to obtain data.

enrichment.problem: The dynamic client’s List method could only perform a standard LIST request, lacking the ability to stream results when a server supports streaming, which could lead to higher latency and less efficient data retrieval for large result sets.
enrichment.affected: Developers using client-go’s dynamic client for List operations, especially those handling large resource collections or requiring lower latency.
enrichment.fix: Added an optional streaming mode to the dynamic client’s List method. Users can enable it by turning on the `client-go.WatchListClient` feature gate; the client will use streaming when the apiserver supports it, otherwise it falls back to the normal LIST call.
enrichment.impact: Clients that need to retrieve large collections can now receive data incrementally, reducing latency and memory usage. The change is backward‑compatible because it automatically falls back if the server does not support streaming.

feature.description: Added a warning log, an event for cgroup v1 usage and a metric for cgroup version.
feature.author: harche
feature.userFacingChange: Add a warning log, an event for cgroup v1 usage and a metric for cgroup version.

enrichment.problem: Clusters running with cgroup v1 have no built-in visibility that they are using a deprecated cgroup version, making it hard for operators to detect and plan migration to cgroup v2.
enrichment.affected: Any node that is configured to use cgroup v1, typically older Linux distributions or custom setups, and the administrators responsible for those nodes.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now emits a warning log and a Node-level event when cgroup v1 is detected, and it publishes a new metric indicating the cgroup version in use.
enrichment.impact: Operators can quickly discover cgroup v1 usage via logs, events, or monitoring dashboards, enabling proactive migration and reducing the risk of future deprecation issues.

feature.description: `--custom` flag in `kubectl debug` will be enabled by default and yaml support is added.
feature.author: ardaguclu
feature.userFacingChange: --custom flag in kubectl debug will be enabled by default and yaml support is added

enrichment.problem: kubectl debug required the --custom flag to be explicitly set to use custom debug containers, and it only supported JSON output, limiting usability for users who wanted custom debugging or yaml-formatted output.
enrichment.affected: Developers and operators using kubectl debug to troubleshoot pods, especially those needing custom debug containers or yaml formatted output.
enrichment.fix: The --custom flag is now enabled by default, removing the need for users to specify it, and yaml output support is added to the command.
enrichment.impact: Users can invoke kubectl debug with custom containers more easily and can request yaml output, improving usability and scriptability of debugging workflows.

feature.description: Built Kubernetes with Go 1.22.4.
feature.author: cpanato
feature.userFacingChange: Kubernetes is now built with go 1.22.4

enrichment.problem: Kubernetes binaries were previously built with an older Go version, which could miss recent compiler improvements, security fixes, and support for newer platforms.
enrichment.affected: All Kubernetes components (kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, kubelet, kubectl, kube-proxy, etc.) built from source are affected as they are now produced with Go 1.22.4.
enrichment.fix: All Kubernetes components are now compiled with Go 1.22.4, updating the toolchain used for building the binaries.
enrichment.impact: Ensures the release benefits from the latest Go compiler optimizations, bug fixes, and security patches, improving reliability and future compatibility for all clusters.

feature.description: LogarithmicScaleDown is now GA.
feature.author: MinpengJin

enrichment.problem: Before this change, the logarithmic scale‑down algorithm for pod autoscaling was only available as an alpha/beta feature, making it unsuitable for production workloads that needed smoother, less aggressive scale‑down behavior.
enrichment.affected: Workloads that use the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, especially those with fluctuating traffic patterns, and any cluster operators deploying autoscaling in production.
enrichment.fix: The LogarithmicScaleDown feature has been promoted to General Availability (GA). It is now a stable, production‑ready option for the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and can be enabled without additional feature‑gate work.
enrichment.impact: Clusters can now use a stable logarithmic scale‑down mechanism, reducing pod churn during rapid load changes and providing more predictable scaling for workloads that rely on the HPA.

feature.description: KEP-3857: promoted RecursiveReadOnlyMounts feature to beta.
feature.author: AkihiroSuda
feature.userFacingChange: KEP-3857: promote RecursiveReadOnlyMounts feature to beta

enrichment.problem: Kubernetes did not support recursive read‑only mounts, preventing users from marking an entire mount tree as read‑only in a single operation. This limited security hardening and required work‑arounds for workloads needing strict read‑only file‑system semantics.
enrichment.affected: Pods that mount volumes and need recursive read‑only enforcement, as well as cluster operators configuring node security policies.
enrichment.fix: The RecursiveReadOnlyMounts feature is promoted to beta. When enabled, kubelet will apply the mount flag MS_RDONLY recursively to all sub‑mounts, allowing pods to declare a volume as read‑only and have the entire subtree enforced as read‑only.
enrichment.impact: Enables a more secure and convenient way to enforce read‑only file‑system semantics for containers. Works for a broader set of use‑cases and reduces the need for custom init containers or privileged work‑arounds.

feature.description:
Delay setting terminal Job conditions until all pods are terminal.

Additionally, the FailureTarget condition is also added to the Job object in the first Job
status update as soon as the failure conditions are met (backoffLimit is exceeded, maxFailedIndexes, 
or activeDeadlineSeconds is exceeded).

Similarly, the SuccessCriteriaMet condition is added in the first update as soon as the expected number
of pod completions is reached.

Also, introduce the following validation rules for Job status when JobManagedBy is enabled:
1. the count of ready pods is less or equal than active
2. when transitioning to terminal phase for Job, the number of terminating pods is 0
3. terminal Job conditions (Failed and Complete) should be preceded by adding the corresponding interim conditions: FailureTarget and SuccessCriteriaMet

issueContext.title: A Job might finish with ready!=0, terminating!=0
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When a Job is declared Failed, the running Pods still count as ready.
This causes problems for higher level controllers that use the Failed/Completed conditions to do usage accounting. If the job is marked as finished before all the pods finish, the accounting is inaccurate.

### What did you expect to happen?

A few options (non-necessarily exclusive), in order of my preference:
1. The job not to be declared Completed/Failed until all the Pods have finished. This is possibly a breaking change. As a mitigation, we can use the `FailureTarget` or `SuccessCriteriaMet` conditions to provide early feedback to controllers that a Job is marked for failure.
2. ~Do not count Pods with a deletionTimestamp as ready. (Possibly a breaking change)~
3. ~We just consider ready=0 if setting a finished condition~
4. Continue syncing a Job even after the Failed condition is added, until ready/terminating fields are zero.

Options 2 and 3 don't satisfy the requirement of proper accounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Use this Job (note backoffLimit: 0):
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: indexed-job
  labels:
    jobgroup: indexedjob
spec:
  completions: 4
  parallelism: 4
  backoffLimit: 0
  completionMode: Indexed
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        jobgroup: indexedjob
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: 'worker'
        image: 'centos:7'
        command:
        - "sh"
        - "-c"
        - "echo 'hello' && sleep 120 && echo 'bye'
```
2. Delete one of the pods with kubectl

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# paste output here
```
ANY
</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
ANY
</details>


### OS version

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-releas

enrichment.problem: Jobs could be marked as Failed or Complete while some of their Pods were still ready or terminating, leading to inaccurate accounting for higher‑level controllers that rely on Job conditions.
enrichment.affected: Users running batch Jobs (including indexed Jobs) and any controllers or tools that depend on Job status for accounting or workflow decisions.
enrichment.fix: The Job controller now delays setting the terminal conditions (Failed, Complete) until all Pods are terminal. It adds interim conditions – FailureTarget when failure criteria (backoffLimit, maxFailedIndexes, activeDeadlineSeconds) are reached, and SuccessCriteriaMet when the expected number of completions is achieved – in the first status update. Additional validation rules are introduced for JobManagedBy: ready pods must not exceed active pods, no terminating pods remain when transitioning to a terminal phase, and interim conditions must precede terminal ones.
enrichment.impact: Higher‑level controllers and users get accurate Job status, preventing premature accounting errors and ensuring that Job lifecycle reflects actual pod termination. The new validation improves consistency and observability of batch jobs.

feature.description:
Enabled feature gates for PortForward (kubectl port-forward) over WebSockets by default (beta).
 - Server-side feature gate: PortForwardWebsocket
 - Client-side (kubectl) feature gate: PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS environment variable
 - To turn off PortForward over WebSockets for kubectl, the environment variable feature gate must be explicitly set - PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS=false
feature.author: seans3
feature.userFacingChange:
- Feature gates for PortForward (kubectl port-forward) over WebSockets are now enabled by default (Beta).
  - Server-side feature gate: PortForwardWebsocket
  - Client-side (kubectl) feature gate: PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS environment variable
  - To turn off PortForward over WebSockets for kubectl, the environment variable feature gate must be explicitly set - PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS=false

enrichment.problem: kubectl port-forward did not use WebSockets by default, requiring manual feature‑gate activation on both the apiserver and client, limiting compatibility with environments that only allow WebSocket traffic.
enrichment.affected: kubectl users performing port-forward and clusters where the apiserver is upgraded; administrators who need to control the feature via environment variable.
enrichment.fix: Enable the PortForwardWebsocket server‑side feature gate and the PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS client‑side feature gate by default (beta). Users can still disable it by setting the environment variable PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS=false.

The change is backward compatible; existing setups continue to work unless they explicitly disable the feature.

enrichment.problem: The fake client-go typed client lacked support for field management and server-side apply, causing unit tests that rely on these features to behave incorrectly or be unable to test managed fields.
enrichment.affected: Developers writing unit tests with client-go's fake client, especially those testing server-side apply or field management logic. Libraries and CI pipelines that use the fake client are also affected.
enrichment.fix: Added field management support to the fake client-go typed client and introduced `fake.NewClientset()` which creates a clientset with managed field support, replacing the previous `fake.NewSimpleClientset()` usage.

feature.description: kubeadm: added the ControlPlaneKubeletLocalMode feature gate. It can be used to tell kubeadm to use the local kube-apiserver endpoint for the kubelet when creating a cluster with "kubeadm init" or when joining control plane nodes with "kubeadm join".  The "kubeadm join" workflow now includes two new experimental phases called "control-plane-join-etcd" and "kubelet-wait-bootstrap" which will be used when the feature gate is enabled. This phases will be marked as non-experimental when ControlPlaneKubeletLocalMode becomes GA. During "kubeadm upgrade" commands, if the feature gate is enabled, modify the "/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf " to use the local kube-apiserver endpoint. This upgrade mechanism will be removed once the feature gate goes GA and is hardcoded to true.
feature.author: chrischdi

enrichment.problem: kubeadm could not configure the kubelet on control‑plane nodes to talk to the local kube‑apiserver endpoint, limiting flexibility for init, join, and upgrade workflows.
enrichment.affected: Users creating or expanding clusters with kubeadm (init, join, upgrade) on control‑plane nodes. The kubelet configuration on those nodes is modified.
enrichment.fix: Introduced the ControlPlaneKubeletLocalMode feature gate. When enabled, kubeadm configures the kubelet to use the local apiserver endpoint during `kubeadm init`, `kubeadm join` (with new experimental phases) and `kubeadm upgrade`, updating `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf` accordingly.
enrichment.impact: Control‑plane nodes can now communicate with the apiserver via the local endpoint, reducing latency and removing reliance on external networking during bootstrap and upgrades. Future GA will make this the default, simplifying cluster setup and upgrade paths.

feature.description: Graduated the `WatchList` feature gate to beta for kube-apiserver and enabled `WatchListClient` for kube-controller-manager (KCM).
feature.author: p0lyn0mial
feature.userFacingChange: Graduates the `WatchList` feature gate to Beta for kube-apiserver and enables `WatchListClient` for KCM.

enrichment.problem: The WatchList feature was only available as an alpha feature gate, limiting its use in production and requiring manual enablement for kube-apiserver and kube-controller-manager.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use watch‑based controllers or custom workloads that depend on watch efficiency were unable to use a stable watch list implementation.
enrichment.fix: Graduates the `WatchList` feature gate to Beta for kube-apiserver and enables the `WatchListClient` for kube-controller-manager, making watch list functionality generally available without extra flags.
enrichment.impact: Users can now rely on stable watch‑list support in production clusters, leading to more efficient watch handling for controllers and reduced overhead when tracking resource changes.

issueContext.title: kubectl not idempotent when setting `null` values
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

As per [this article](https://home.robusta.dev/blog/stop-using-cpu-limits), I'm trying to remove CPU limits.

But the behaviour is different depending whether the ResourceQuota exists or not:

```
$ kubectl describe quota
No resources found in deleteme namespace.

$ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
kind: ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: compute-resources
  namespace: deleteme
spec:
  hard:
    limits.cpu: null
EOF
resourcequota/compute-resources created

$ kubectl describe quota
Name:       compute-resources
Namespace:  deleteme
Resource    Used  Hard
--------    ----  ----
limits.cpu  0     0

$ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
kind: ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: compute-resources
  namespace: deleteme
spec:
  hard:
    limits.cpu: null
EOF
resourcequota/compute-resources configured

$ kubectl describe quota
Name:       compute-resources
Namespace:  deleteme
Resource    Used  Hard
--------    ----  ----
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect `kubectl` to be idempotent, and for its behaviour to result in the same end configuration regardless of the initial configuration.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a new namespace named `deleteme`
2. Run this command:

   ```
   kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
   kind: ResourceQuota
   apiVersion: v1
   metadata:
     name: compute-resources
     namespace: deleteme
   spec:
     hard:
       limits.cpu: null
   EOF
   ```

3. Observe that the ResourceQuota is created and `limits.cpu` is set to `0`
4. Run it again
5. Observe that `limits.cpu` is removed each subsequent time it's run, as long as resourcequota/compute-resource exists
6. Delete resourcequota/compute-resource
7. Run `kubectl apply` again
8. Observe that the ResourceQuota is created and `limits.cpu` is set to `0` again, and so forth
9. Observe the exact same behaviour if `limits.cpu: null` is changed to `limi

enrichment.problem: kubectl client-side apply treated a null value as a regular field on creation, leading to non‑idempotent behavior (e.g., applying a ResourceQuota with limits.cpu: null created a hard limit of 0, while a subsequent apply removed the key).
enrichment.affected: Any workflow that uses `kubectl apply` to set fields to null, especially for ResourceQuota and similar resources, where the object may or may not already exist.
enrichment.fix: The client‑side apply logic was changed so that a null value is interpreted as a delete operation even on object creation, making the apply idempotent.
enrichment.impact: Users can reliably use `kubectl apply` with null values to remove fields (such as CPU limits) without unexpected side effects, improving configuration stability and automation scripts.

feature.description: `ElasticIndexedJob` is graduated to GA.
feature.author: ahg-g
feature.userFacingChange: ElasticIndexedJob is graduated to GA

issueContext.title: Elastic Indexed Job
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently we validate that `spec.completions` is set when `completionMode=Indexed` for job. I suggest we relax this validation. 

This will require the following changes:

1) We need to update the job controller to look at `spec.parallelism` instead of `spec.completions` when calculating the range of indexes.
2) When reducing parallelism, we should remove the higher indexes first (otherwise the controller will eventually do that anyways to ensure that the pods have a continuous range).

both changes only apply when `spec.completions=nil`

### Why is this needed?

The use case is jobs with workers that require a form of autoscaling, like Ray, Spark or Horovord. By modeling these as jobs with `spec.completion=nil`, `spec.parallelism` can be used to scale the job.

While such jobs could be modeled as a StatefulSet, the job API offers batch-specific features that makes it a better fit (like [retriable and non retriable failures](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/3329-retriable-and-non-retriable-failures))

/sig apps
@soltysh @alculquicondor wdyt?

enrichment.problem: Jobs using completionMode=Indexed required spec.completions to be set, preventing autoscaling scenarios where the desired number of parallel pods changes dynamically (e.g., Ray, Spark, Horovod).
enrichment.affected: Users running Indexed completion mode jobs that need elastic scaling (e.g., machine‑learning or data‑processing frameworks).
enrichment.fix: The ElasticIndexedJob feature is graduated to GA. Validation is relaxed so spec.completions may be omitted. The job controller now uses spec.parallelism to determine index ranges and removes higher indexes first when scaling down.
enrichment.impact: Enables elastic, indexed batch jobs to scale automatically, broadening the use cases for Jobs and allowing workloads that need dynamic parallelism to use the Job API with full batch semantics.

enrichment.problem: There was no explicit way for users to indicate whether a pod is ready to be considered for scheduling, causing the scheduler to potentially attempt to place pods that are not yet ready (e.g., waiting on init containers or external provisioning).
enrichment.affected: All pods that rely on init containers, external provisioning, or custom controllers that need to gate scheduling until certain conditions are met.
enrichment.fix: Introduces a new `PodSchedulingReadiness` condition in the Pod API that can be set by controllers or users. The scheduler now checks this condition and will only schedule pods whose condition is `True`. The apiserver schema and validation are updated accordingly.
enrichment.impact: Provides finer‑grained control over when a pod becomes eligible for scheduling, preventing premature placement attempts and reducing scheduling failures or unnecessary rescheduling cycles. Improves overall cluster stability and predictability for workloads that have preparatory steps before they can be scheduled.

feature.description: Promoted CRI communication of the cgroup driver mechanism to beta. The `KubeletCgroupDriverFromCRI` feature gate is now in beta and enabled by default. This allows the kubelet to query the container runtime using CRI to determine the mechanism for cgroup management. If the container runtime doesn't support this, the kubelet falls back to using the configuration file (you can also use the deprecated `--cgroup-driver` command line argument).
feature.author: haircommander
feature.userFacingChange:
Promoted CRI communication of cgroup driver mechanism, to beta.
The `KubeletCgroupDriverFromCRI` feature gate is now beta and enabled by default. This means that the kubelet queries the container runtime using CRI to discover the mechanism for cgroup management that the kubelet will use; if the container runtime doesn't support this, the kubelet falls back to loading this from its configuration file (you can also use the deprecated `--cgroup-driver` command line argument).

enrichment.problem: The kubelet needed an explicit configuration of the cgroup driver, which could become out‑of‑sync with the container runtime, leading to cgroup management errors or manual configuration burdens.
enrichment.affected: Kubernetes clusters where the kubelet and container runtime must share the same cgroup driver configuration, especially those that previously relied on manual flags or config files.
enrichment.fix: The KubeletCgroupDriverFromCRI feature gate is promoted to beta and enabled by default. The kubelet now queries the container runtime via CRI to discover the cgroup driver mechanism, falling back to the config file or deprecated `--cgroup-driver` flag if the runtime does not support the query.
enrichment.impact: Clusters automatically align the kubelet’s cgroup driver with the container runtime, reducing misconfiguration risk and simplifying upgrades. Existing workflows continue to work via the fallback mechanisms.

feature.description: The Service trafficDistribution field has graduated to beta and is now available for configuration by default, without the need to enable any feature flag. enrichment.fix: The `trafficDistribution` field has been graduated to beta and is now enabled by default, allowing clusters to configure traffic distribution for Services without any feature flag. Existing Services without the field continue to behave as before.

feature.description: kube-apiserver: when the Alpha `UserNamespacesPodSecurityStandards` feature gate is enabled, Pod Security Admission enforcement of the baseline policy now allows `procMount: Unmasked` for user namespace pods that set `hostUsers: false`.

issueContext.title: When PreFilter's PreFilterResult filter out some Nodes, unschedulable plugin isn't registered for those plugins
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

from: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118369#issuecomment-1581610018

When PreFilter's PreFilterResult filters out some Nodes, unschedulable plugin isn't registered for those plugins. 

1. PreFilterA filters out all Nodes but NodeA via PreFilterResult.
2. FilterA filters out NodeA.
3. Currently, only FilterA is registered in unsched plugins.

issueContext.title: Daemonset RollingUpdate does not correctly count old non-ready pods towards MaxUnavailable budget
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Starting with a cluster of three nodes, with a healthy deamonset pod running on each, with `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable=1`.
```
kubectl get pods
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-7fmn7   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-mflls   1/1     Running   0          17s          
```

When performing three updates to the daemonset, each with some reason that prevents the new pods from becoming ready, I  ended up with zero ready pods.
```
kubectl get pods                                                                                                                                               
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-5sbf5   0/1     Running   0          9s
demo-daemonset-bswfc   0/1     Running   0          9s
demo-daemonset-jgdv7   0/1     Running   0          9s
```


### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect that when I apply an update, and the new pods fail to become ready, when I apply a second update the "new" failing pods are replaced before considering any of the oldest healthy pods.
This is similar behavior to how Deployments work.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a three node (or any count really) cluster, create this daemonset, which is just an nginx pod with a startup probe hitting port 80.
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: demo-daemonset
  namespace: 
  labels:
    app: demo-daemonset
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo-daemonset
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo-daemonset
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:latest
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80

enrichment.problem: During a DaemonSet rolling update, the controller ignored old pods that were already unhealthy when calculating the maxUnavailable budget. This allowed the number of unavailable pods to exceed the configured limit, potentially leaving all DaemonSet pods non‑ready.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using DaemonSets with rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable; workloads that rely on DaemonSets for node‑level services could have experienced temporary service loss during problematic rollouts.
enrichment.fix: The DaemonSet controller logic was changed to include old unhealthy (non‑ready) pods in the maxUnavailable count, ensuring the budget is respected during rollouts.
enrichment.impact: Rollouts of DaemonSets with a rollingUpdate strategy now correctly honor maxUnavailable, preventing full‑scale downtime and making DaemonSet behavior consistent with Deployments.

issueContext.title: RecreatingTerminatedPod/RecreatingFailedPod/SuccessfulDelete events leak
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

The event `RecreatingTerminatedPod` is emitted ~10 times simultaneously after evicting pods of a Statefulset.



### What did you expect to happen?

The event should only be emitted at most once.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a 1.29 kind cluster:
```
kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.29
```
 (tested with `sha256:eaa1450915475849a73a9227b8f201df25e55e268e5d619312131292e324d570`)

- Deploy a statefulset:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          name: web
```

- Get the initial `RecreatingTerminatedPod` event count for that sts:
```
kubectl get events  --field-selector involvedObject.kind=StatefulSet,involvedObject.name=web,reason=RecreatingTerminatedPod -o json | jq '.items[].count'
```
(shoud return nothing)

- Taint the node:
```
kubectl taint nodes kind-control-plane foo=bar:NoExecute
```

- Get the event count now:
```
kubectl get events  --field-selector involvedObject.kind=StatefulSet,involvedObject.name=web,reason=RecreatingTerminatedPod -o json | jq '.items[].count'
```
(got: `10`, `11`,`9`...)

### Anything else we need to know?

From the kube-controller logs:

```

2024-01-11T11:26:09.135572053Z I0111 11:26:09.135506       1 event.go:376] "Event occurred" object="default/web" fieldPath="" kind="StatefulSet" apiVersion="apps/v1" type="Normal" reason="SuccessfulDelete" messa

enrichment.problem: StatefulSet controller emitted RecreatingFailedPod and RecreatingTerminatedPod events multiple times (event leak) during pod eviction or failure, leading to noisy and misleading event counts.
enrichment.affected: Any cluster running StatefulSets, especially when pods are terminated or fail. Event watchers, dashboards, and alerting systems that consumed RecreatingFailedPod/RecreatingTerminatedPod events.

issueContext.title: kubelet: Evicted and force deleted pods get their full termination grace period when they should not
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When pods are evicted, i.e. with a hard eviction, the grace period is intended to be `0s` (i.e. do not respect the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`). 

However, currently, evicted pods receive their full termination grace period seconds.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod is evicted immediately and the termination grace period is not respected 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the following pod which has an ephemeral storage limit of 5Mi and uses `dd` to fill the disk

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: evictdiskpod
  labels:
    pod: evictdiskpod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    resources:
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: 5Mi
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            echo "Caught SIGTERM signal!"
            while true; do sleep 5; done
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM
        sleep 10
        dd if=/dev/zero of=file bs=1M count=10
        echo 'write done'
        while true; do sleep 5; done
```

2. Observe the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds was respected when it should've not been

In the logs:

```
# I added a debug print to include grace period here (it is zero)

Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.688937     275 pod_workers.go:906] "Processing pod e

enrichment.problem: When a pod is hard evicted due to node resource pressure, or when a pod is force‑deleted, the kubelet incorrectly applied the pod's full `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` instead of terminating the pod immediately.
enrichment.affected: Pods that are hard‑evicted because of node resource pressure and pods that are force‑deleted. The behavior impacted nodes running the kubelet.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now overrides the grace period for hard‑evicted and force‑deleted pods, assigning a termination grace period of 1 second so the pod shuts down essentially instantly.
enrichment.impact: Pods are removed promptly after eviction or force‑deletion, freeing node resources faster and avoiding unnecessary delays that could impede node recovery or cause resource contention.

issueContext.title: PersistentVolumeLabel admission blocks PVs on Azure + vSphere
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

In 1.30, the PersistentVolumeLabel admission plugin blocks creation of in-tree AzureDisk and vSphere PVs:

```
persistentvolumes "pvc-2d9b3999-f60d-4797-923f-210f1f75025d" is forbidden:
error querying AzureDisk volume pvc-2d9b3999-f60d-4797-923f-210f1f75025d:
unable to build Azure cloud provider for AzureDisk
```

The reason is that the cloud provider was removed (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122857), but the admission plugin still calls GetCloudProvider there, which fails: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/646fbe6d0a3fa1a100d90a429f039324de9c8138/plugin/pkg/admission/storage/persistentvolume/label/admission.go#L285


### What did you expect to happen?

The PV should be admitted + created.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable PersistentVolumeLabel admission plugin. For example, when running local-up-cluster.sh:
```
ALLOW_PRIVILEGED=true ENABLE_ADMISSION_PLUGINS="NamespaceLifecycle,LimitRanger,ServiceAccount,DefaultStorageClass,DefaultTolerationSeconds,Priority,MutatingAdmissionWebhook,ValidatingAdmissionWebhook,ResourceQuota,NodeRestriction,PersistentVolumeLabel" bash -x hack/local-up-cluster.sh
```

Create AzureDisk PV on _any_ 1.30 cluster, you don't need Azure cloud:

```
kubectl create -f <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: myvol
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  capacity:
    storage: 5Gi
  azureDisk:
    diskName: test2.vhd
    diskURI: https://someacount.blob.core.windows.net/vhds/test2.vhd
EOF
```

### Anything else we need to know?

/sig storage
/priority important-soon

### Kubernetes version

<details>

Today's master
```console
$ kubectl version
Server Version: v1.31.0-alpha.0.24+9791f0d1f39f3f
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
Azure
</details>


### OS version

_No response_

### Install tools

<details>
local-up-cluster.sh
</details>


###

### Problem statement

Using `code-generator`'s `client-gen` in version 1.30 adds several new fields to generated CRDs:

```diff
                           imagePullSecrets:
                             description: |-

                             items:
                               description: |-

                                 referenced object inside the same namespace.
                               properties:
                                 name:
                                   description: |-
                                     Name of the referent.
                                     More info: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names/#names

issueContext.title: Scheduler throughput reduced when many gated pods
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When handling a delete pod event, we attempt to remove pods from the unscheduablePods pool [1], taking a lock while doing so [2]. Gated pods reside in this unscheduable pool, and we process all of them for each delete event. Scheduling throughput is affected, likely because ScheduleOne also takes a lock [3]

[1] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/00117569f3ab6456791c4e65fc4543a4278d1332/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L244-L249

[2] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/00117569f3ab6456791c4e65fc4543a4278d1332/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L1093-L1097

[3] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/00117569f3ab6456791c4e65fc4543a4278d1332/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L69


### What did you expect to happen?

Scheduling throughput should not reduce when there are many gated pods. We eventually decide against moving these pods, but after some processing. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/be4b7176dc131ea842cab6882cd4a06dbfeed12a/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L1178-L1183

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create many (~10000) gated pods. Then, create non-gated pods which eventually terminate. As these pods finish and pod delete events are processed, scheduling throughput decreases

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Server Version: v1.29.1-gke.1589017
```
</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
Google Cloud - GKE
</details>


### OS version

_No response_

### Install tools

_No response_

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

_No response_

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

_No response_

enrichment.problem: When many gated pods are present, the scheduler locks the unschedulable pod pool for each pod delete event and processes all gated pods, causing lock contention and reduced scheduling throughput and latency.
enrichment.affected: Kubernetes clusters that create large numbers of gated pods (e.g., pending due to node selectors, affinities, or other constraints) and experience frequent pod deletions.
enrichment.fix: The scheduler logic was updated to handle delete events more efficiently, reducing the amount of work and lock contention for gated pods in the unschedulable pool, which improves scheduling latency when many gated pods trigger requeueing.
enrichment.impact: Clusters with large numbers of gated (unschedulable) pods will see faster pod scheduling and higher overall throughput, preventing performance regressions during normal pod churn.

bugOrRegression.description: kube-apiserver: the `--encryption-provider-config` file is now loaded with strict deserialization, which fails if the config file contains duplicate or unknown fields. bugOrRegression.author: enj

enrichment.problem: The kube-apiserver accepted encryption provider configuration files that contained duplicate or unknown fields, and with automatic reload it could silently accept malformed new configs, leading to unexpected or insecure encryption behavior.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using kube-apiserver encryption provider configs, especially those enabling automatic reload, could experience incorrect encryption if the config contained typos or duplicate fields.

bugOrRegression.description: Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA): using structured parameters with a claim that gets reused between pods may have led to a claim with an invalid state (allocated without a finalizer) which then caused scheduling of pods using the claim to stop.

bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: DRA: using structured parameters with a claim that gets reused between pods may have led to a claim with an invalid state (allocated without a finalizer) which then caused scheduling of pods using the claim to stop.

enrichment.problem: When a Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) claim that uses structured parameters is reused across multiple pods, the claim could end up in an invalid state – it becomes allocated but lacks the required finalizer. enrichment.fix: The DRA implementation now correctly adds and preserves the finalizer on allocated claims even when the claim is reused with structured parameters. The scheduler’s handling of DRA claims is updated to recognize and recover from this situation, restoring normal pod scheduling.
enrichment.impact: Workloads that rely on DRA (e.g., CSI drivers supporting dynamic resource allocation) and reuse claims across pods will no longer get stuck in a pending state. Pods can be scheduled again, reducing downtime and improving reliability of resource‑intensive applications.

### What happened?

We upgraded our test cluster to `1.28.8` (GKE `1.28.8-gke.1095000`) and noticed that some of our tests began to time out when watching for events that never arrived. 

Upon investigation, it appears that there is a regression in the deprecated path-based watch API for at least `namespaces` e.g. `http://localhost:8001/api/v1/watch/namespaces/<name>`. We have not been able to reproduce this with any other resource type.

When creating a watch for a namespace (see `how to reproduce`) we see the initial `added` event, but then we do not see subsequent events if we modify the namespace e.g. add a label or annotation. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect to see events when the namespace is altered. E.g. adding a label should produce a `MODIFIED` event with the contents.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a new test namespace e.g. `kubectl create namespace test-namespace`
2. Create a proxy to the master `kubectl proxy`
3. Curl the watch path of the namespace that has been created e.g. `http://localhost:8001/api/v1/watch/namespaces/test-namespace`
4. In another shell, modify the namespace to add a label to it.
5. Observe that there is no modified event in the watch.

### Anything else we need to know?

It is understood that the `/watch` based paths are and have been for some time deprecated, we are working on moving to use the watch query param instead.

issueContext.title: ResourceClaimParametersRef.APIGroup allows APIversion values
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Following YAML file is accepted without error. Notice the `spec.parametersRef.apiGroup` field, it is an `APIVersion` instead of `APIGroup`, containing `/` character. This can lead to an issue when resource driver generates structured parameters' in-tree `ResourceClaimParameters` object with `generatedFrom.apiGroup` being just `APIGroup` without version. The DRA scheduler plugin will try to match the parameters object based on the reference here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/be4afb9ef90b19ccb6f7e595cbdb247e088b2347/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go#L1066

In latest master the code appears to use an indexer, and the issue might be hidden, if applicable at all. I did not check the reproducibility in master yet. However, main question is whether the `APIGroup` should allow `APIVersion` value with `/` character in general.

```YAML
apiVersion: gpu.resource.intel.com/v1alpha2
kind: GpuClaimParameters
metadata:
  name: delayed-claim-external-gpu
spec:
  count: 1
  type: "gpu"
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: delayed-claim-external-gpu
spec:
  resourceClassName: intel-gpu-structured
  parametersRef:
    apiGroup: gpu.resource.intel.com/v1alpha2
    kind: GpuClaimParameters
    name: delayed-claim-external-gpu
```

### What did you expect to happen?

An error is expected from the apiserver upon object creation request, reporting that APIGroup containes APIVersion. Maybe.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Have any resource driver that supports structured parameters, [dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/pull/47/files#diff-df3210fefbab9f26fa97ba679b29869e25ce897d0ba713ce461da521f10ff7d8), for instance, also puts `APIGroup` (gpucrd.APIGroup) value into `generatedFrom.apiGroup`.

### Anything else we need to know?

### Kubernetes version

v1.30.1

#

enrichment.problem: The apiserver allowed invalid values for ResourceClaimParametersReference and ResourceClassParametersReference fields (apiGroup, kind, name). Users could set apiGroup to an APIVersion containing '/' or use '.' '..' '/' '%' in kind/name, causing the DRA scheduler plugin to fail matching the parameters object, leading to scheduling failures for pods using DRA.
enrichment.affected: Users creating ResourceClaim or ResourceClass objects with DRA where the parameters reference contained an invalid apiGroup or illegal characters in kind/name. Clusters using DRA drivers were at risk of unschedulable pods.
enrichment.fix: Added strict validation for these references: if apiGroup is set it must be a valid DNS subdomain; kind and name must be valid path segment names and cannot be '.' or '..' or contain '/' or '%' characters. Invalid objects are rejected by the apiserver.
enrichment.impact: Prevents creation of malformed ResourceClaim objects, ensuring the DRA scheduler can reliably locate the corresponding ResourceClaimParameters. Users of Dynamic Resource Allocator will see early validation errors instead of silent scheduling failures.

issueContext.title: Server-side apply has trouble with empty map
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Every time I server-side apply a `Deployment` with `spec.template.metadata.annotations: {}`, the `resourceVersion` updates. Nothing about my manifest changes between applies; if I map `annotations` to the empty map, `kubectl apply --server-side` the same manifest updates the `resourceVersion`. With client-side apply, the `resourceVersion` stays the same as long as my manifest remains constant, even if `annotations: {}`.

I read in #70281 that Kubernetes should treat absent keys, empty values (in this case, an empty map), and `null` values the same. I observe that leaving the `annotations` key out and `annotations: null` behave as expected, not modifying the `Deployment` and leaving `resourceVersion` the same, but empty map `{}` behaves as described above.

If we cannot change this behavior, I'd at least like to understand the rationale behind it.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected my `Deployment` object to stay the same between identical server-side applies, where the manifest file content was exactly the same, regardless of the value of `spec.template.metadata.annotations`. A different `resourceVersion` every apply indicates that the object was event type `MODIFIED`. I expect no events to fire on applying the same manifest.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Say `deployment.yaml` contains https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#creating-a-deployment. In actuality, any `Deployment` is fine.
2. Add `spec.template.metadata.annotatations: {}`.
3. `kubectl apply --server-side deployment.yaml`
4. `kubectl get deployment nginx-deployment -o yaml`

Every successive repeat of steps 3-4 should show different `metadata.resourceVersion` values.

Example of `Deployment` with `spec.template.metadata.annotatations: {}`:
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selecto

issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When Job controller is deleting pods the counter in the status.ready field does not reflect this properly (there is a delay until the cache is refreshed). This affects the scenarios of terminating job, suspended job, and excess pods deleted.

### What did you expect to happen?

The ready field is updated as soon as the delete requests are sent successfully, in sync with the status.active field.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. To see this you can scale down a job, use the following yaml:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: simple-job
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: 'worker'
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import time
          time.sleep(300)
```

2. Watch for the job updates with the following watcher:
```
kubectl get jobs -w --output-watch-events -ocustom-columns=EVENT:.type,NAME:.object.metadata.name,READY:.object.status.ready,ACTIVE:.object.status.active,TERMINATING:.object.status.terminating,CONDITIONS:.object.status.conditions | ts "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%.S"`
```
3. Scale down the job by `kubectl edit job` and decrease parallelism and completions to 1.

We observe events like the following
```

2024-05-29 12:49:58.810008 MODIFIED   simple-job   0        2        0             <none>
2024-05-29 12:50:02.065710 MODIFIED   simple-job   2        2        0             <none>
2024-05-29 12:50:17.526562 MODIFIED   simple-job   2        2        0             <none>
2024-05-29 12:50:17.542893 MODIFIED   simple-job   2        1        0             <none>
2024-05-29 12:50:18.537404 MODIFIED   simple-job   1        1        1             <none>
2024-05-29 12:50:48.785143 MODIFIED   simple

enrichment.problem: The Job controller's .status.ready field was not updated promptly when active Pods were deleted (e.g., job failure, suspension, or excess pods). The status remained stale until the cache refreshed, causing a delay in reflecting the true ready pod count.
enrichment.affected: Jobs that use parallelism/completions (including indexed jobs) and scenarios where jobs are scaled down, fail, or are suspended. Controllers and dashboards that rely on .status.ready for job health were affected.
enrichment.fix: The controller now increments/decrements the .status.ready count immediately when delete requests for Pods are successfully issued, keeping it in sync with .status.active. This speeds up readiness tracking for jobs undergoing pod deletions.
enrichment.impact: Users monitoring Job progress see accurate ready pod counts right after scaling down, failures, or suspensions, improving observability and preventing misleading job status information.

bugOrRegression.description:

bugOrRegression.author: carlory
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange:
For statically provisioned PVs, if its volume source is CSI type or it has migrated annotation, when it's deleted, the PersisentVolume controller won't changes its phase to the Failed state. 

With this patch, the external provisioner can remove the finalizer in next reconcile loop. Unfortunately if the provious existing pv has the Failed state, this patch won't take effort. It requires users to remove finalizer.

enrichment.problem: When a statically provisioned PersistentVolume that uses a CSI volume source or has the migrated annotation is deleted, the PersistentVolume controller fails to set its phase to Failed, leaving the PV's finalizer in place and preventing automatic cleanup by the external provisioner.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use statically provisioned PersistentVolumes backed by CSI drivers or with the migrated annotation. Administrators who delete such PVs were previously unable to fully clean them up.
enrichment.fix: The controller logic is updated to set the PV phase to Failed for those CSI or migrated static PVs during deletion, allowing the external provisioner to remove the finalizer in the next reconcile loop. Existing PVs already in Failed state still require manual finalizer removal.
enrichment.impact: Stuck PersistentVolumes are now cleaned up automatically, preventing resource leakage and reducing manual intervention for administrators managing static CSI PVs.

issueContext.title: Remove Kubelet soft-admission
issueContext.body:
Kubelet soft admission handlers were created as a way for the Kubelet to block pods that cannot be run for reasons that can be resolved. In practice, this mechanism was only ever used by AppArmor ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/eef6c6082d4e34fc4a0675a36ec5cc575cd13696/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L912)).

Problems with soft-admission rejection:
1. This is only used by AppArmor, and only for situations that cannot realistically be resolved (host or build does not support apparmor)
2. Pods held in the blocked state must be manually cleaned up. While there they hold reserved capacity from the scheduler and continually retry syncpod.
3. No other features work this way - usually Kubelet hard rejects pods that it knows it cannot run, or the runtime fails to start the pod/container.

This was originally added to prevent controllers from continuously recreating pods that cannot run, but that is a separate problem that should be approached globally, rather than with this 1-off AppArmor solution.

I propose we remove Kubelet soft admission entirely, and move the AppArmor admission handler to the hard-admission list.

/sig node
/milestone v1.31
/kind bug

enrichment.problem: Kubelet used a soft‑admission handler for AppArmor. When a node did not have AppArmor enabled, pods that requested AppArmor profiles were placed in a blocked state instead of being rejected. Those blocked pods remained queued, reserved scheduler capacity, and required manual cleanup.
enrichment.affected: Workloads that request AppArmor profiles on nodes where AppArmor is not enabled, and the nodes themselves because they now reject such pods during admission.
enrichment.fix: Removed the soft‑admission handler and moved the AppArmor check to hard‑admission. Kubelet now immediately rejects pods that specify an AppArmor profile on nodes without AppArmor support, preventing them from being admitted at all.
enrichment.impact: Pods that cannot be run due to missing AppArmor are rejected at admission time, freeing scheduler capacity and eliminating stuck, blocked pods that required manual cleanup. Controllers receive a clear error, enabling proper remediation.

bugOrRegression.description: Enforced kubelet to request serving certificates only once it has at least one IP address in the `.status.addresses` of its associated Node object. This avoids requesting DNS-only serving certificates before externally set addresses are in place. Until 1.33, the previous behavior can be opted back into by setting the deprecated `AllowDNSOnlyNodeCSR` feature gate to true in the kubelet.
bugOrRegression.author: aojea
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: kubelet now requests serving certificates only once it has at least one IP address in the `.status.addresses` of its associated Node object. This avoids requesting DNS-only serving certificates before externally set addresses are in place. Until 1.33, the previous behavior can be opted back into by setting the deprecated AllowDNSOnlyNodeCSR feature gate to true in the kubelet.

enrichment.problem: The kubelet could request serving certificates before the node object had any IP address in .status.addresses, resulting in DNS‑only certificates that may be invalid for nodes that later receive externally set IP addresses.
enrichment.affected: Nodes that start the kubelet before an IP address is populated (e.g., clusters using external/cloud‑provider address assignment) and any workloads that depend on node serving certificates.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now waits until the associated Node object reports at least one IP address before requesting its serving certificate. The previous behavior can be re‑enabled (until v1.33) via the deprecated AllowDNSOnlyNodeCSR feature gate.
enrichment.impact: Ensures node serving certificates include IP SANs, preventing connection failures or mis‑configurations caused by DNS‑only certificates. Improves reliability of node authentication without requiring manual intervention.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed a bug that init containers with `Always` restartPolicy may not terminate gracefully if the pod hasn't initialized yet.
bugOrRegression.author: gjkim42

issueContext.title: Termination signals not sent to Native Sidecars when multiple Native Sidecars
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

In a situation where during the init phase of a `Pod`, a native sidecar never becomes ready (because its `startupProbe` is failing), then the `Pod` is terminated, if there are multiple startup containers, a termination signal is never received by the init container and the Pod is stuck (until `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is hit).

### What did you expect to happen?

All running initContainer to receive the termination signal correctly.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a `Dockerfile` with this bash script as an entrypoint:

```
#!/bin/bash
set -e 
trap 'echo "saw an exit signal"; sleep 5; exit' EXIT

while true; do
  echo "hello"
  sleep 1
done
```

Create a deployment with two init containers (one normal one sidecar).  Add an probe which means the startupProbe never passes

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: karl-test-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app2: karl-test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app2: karl-test 
    spec:
      securityContext:
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 600
      initContainers:
      - name: init-1
        image: eu.gcr.io/at-artefacts/karl-test
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        command: ["sh", "-c", "echo 'init container 1'"]
      - name: init-2
        image: eu.gcr.io/at-artefacts/karl-test
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        restartPolicy: Always 
        startupProbe:                                                                                                                                                                                                          
          failureThreshold: 600 
          httpGet:
            path: /whatever
            port: 1234
            scheme: HTTP
          periodSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1

enrichment.problem: Init containers with restartPolicy=Always could fail to receive termination signals when the pod is being terminated before the init phase completes, especially with multiple init containers or native sidecars, causing pods to hang until terminationGracePeriodSeconds expires.
enrichment.affected: Workloads that use init containers with restartPolicy=Always, particularly those that include native sidecars or multiple init containers, may have experienced delayed termination.
enrichment.fix: The kubelet logic was corrected to ensure termination signals are delivered to all running init containers regardless of the pod's initialization state, allowing graceful shutdown even with restartPolicy=Always.
enrichment.impact: Pods no longer get stuck during termination, reducing wait times, freeing resources promptly, and improving reliability for workloads that use init containers and sidecars.

issueContext.title: Unable to deploy sample-apiserver: emulation version 1.32 is not between [1.30, 1.31.0]
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Following the instructions in https://github.com/kubernetes/sample-apiserver/blob/master/README.md:
1. Built the sample-apiserver image using the tip of the master branch (dd24c9e2a45c5d0eb7a98a2246906f6e2ec7c0e7)
2. Deployed the sample-apiserver image into a kind cluster.

The deployment failed with
```
$ k logs wardle-server-65dbc6f5d-9pwv4 -n wardle
Defaulted container "wardle-server" out of: wardle-server, etcd
I0707 11:16:37.994750       1 registry.go:379] setting wardle:feature gate emulation version to 1.2
I0707 11:16:37.997302       1 registry.go:379] setting kube:feature gate emulation version to 1.32
I0707 11:16:37.997370       1 feature_gate.go:522] set feature gate emulationVersion to 1.32
I0707 11:16:37.998443       1 plugins.go:83] "Registered admission plugin" plugin="BanFlunder"
E0707 11:16:38.001481       1 run.go:72] "command failed" err="emulation version 1.32 is not between [1.30, 1.31.0]"
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Deployment succeeds. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kubernetes/sample-apiserver.git
cd sample-apiserver
IMAGE=...
podman build -t $IMAGE ./artifacts/simple-image
podman push $IMAGE
# Adjust deployment.yaml to use the image built previously, then apply the manifests
kubectl apply -f artifacts/example
```

Now check pods in the wardle namespace. 

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.29.3
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Server Version: v1.30.2
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

KIND.

enrichment.problem: When deploying the sample-apiserver built from the latest master, the apiserver rejects the request because the feature gate emulation version 1.32 is outside the supported range [1.30, 1.31.0], causing the pod to crash.
